Description: This measure shows the average ambient air temperature in Fahrenheit taken on July 28th, 2023, for each census tract in Chicago through an intitative that brought government agencies, academics, and community members together to model urban heat islands on the hottest day of the year at that time.

This Chicago EJ index is a composite score that measures the cumulative impacts reflecting communities most burdened by pollution and most vulnerable to its effects. Higher values indicate greater burden and vulnerability.

Economic hardship is measured as a composite index from six measures: unemployment, dependency, education, income, crowded housing, poverty. This index measure compares economic conditions between communities in a more comprehensive way than a single measure could.
Data Source(s): American Community Survey via HeRoP Lab, Nathan and Adams (1976)

Description: Green infrastructure like increased tree canopy can reduce the negative impacts of air pollution and extreme heat. This measure estimates the percentage of total census tract area covered by tree canopy in 2017. Using LiDAR technology and multiple geoprocessing steps, a gridded surface covered by a tree’s branches and leaves were created. The final results were then aggregated to percent of census tract covered by canopy.
Data Source(s): Original data from Chicago Region Trees Initiative (CRTI) and funded by The Morton Arboretum, US Forest Service, and American Forest. Aggregated to tracts by HeRoP Lab.
Added By: Lindsay Darling @Chicago Regions Tree Initiative, Catherine Discenza at HEROP Lab@UIUC

Description: Redlining maps of US cities were originally created by the Home Owners’ Loan Corporation (HOLC) in the 1930s. Neighborhoods were assigned to one of four categories: A - “Best,” B - “Still Desirable,” C - “Definitely Declining,” or D - “Hazardous.” This variable reports which of the four categories was assigned to the most area within each tract, for all tracts in which over 50% of the tract area was categorized. Residents in areas marked C or D were frequently denied financial and other services, and the legacy of discrimination against these areas persist materially today.
